The projection documents meaningful federal welfare action and measurable gains: multidimensional poverty and child poverty declined, transfers reduced exposure, learning-recovery camps addressed COVID-era losses, and evaluation institutions remained active (E076, E077, E080, E081, E082). These are concrete ruler-attributable policies with evidence of delivery or outcome, supporting a score above failure or neutrality. However, the portfolio was not broadly equitable or reliably implemented. Health-service deprivation reached 39.1% nationally and 54.8% rurally, Indigenous-language speakers with at least three deprivations increased, and medicine shortages persisted amid executive-centralized procurement (E078, E079, E085). The transfer architecture also raised targeting and clientelism concerns, without decisive proof of loyalty conditioning (E083, E084). Attribution is meaningful for federal policy design and management, but shared with states, inherited fragmentation, and pandemic recovery. A 6.5 or higher is rejected because quality, equity, and durability are insufficiently demonstrated; 4.5 or lower is rejected because real gains and active mitigation are
